# Philip Rubin
Philip Rubin is a distinguished researcher in experimental psychology, linguistics, and speech technology, best known for his foundational work in articulatory synthesis and the biological bases of speech and language. He earned his BA from Brandeis University and his PhD from the University of Connecticut under the tutelage of Michael Turvey, Ignatius Mattingly, Philip Lieberman, and Alvin Liberman. Rubin's research spans computational, engineering, linguistic, physiological, and psychological approaches, focusing on embodied cognition and the spatiotemporal coordination of speech gestures. He is particularly renowned for developing the ASY (articulatory synthesis) and SWS (sinewave synthesis) programs at Haskins Laboratories, as well as the HADES signal processing system and the SPIEL programming language, a predecessor to MATLAB.
Beyond his technical contributions, Rubin has held significant leadership roles in science administration and policy. From 2000 to 2003, he served as the Director of the Division of Behavioral and Cognitive Sciences at the National Science Foundation (NSF), where he launched several key programs including Cognitive Neuroscience and Human Origins. He later returned to the NSF as a senior advisor during the Obama administration and subsequently became the Assistant Director for Social, Behavioral, and Economic Sciences at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) in 2012. At OSTP, he led the White House's neuroscience initiative and co-chaired various interagency working groups, including the NSTC Committee on Science and the Human Subjects Research Working Group. Rubin is also a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and has been actively involved in science advocacy, ethics, and education throughout his career.
